Abigail Bradshaw says ‘enormous’ amounts of money required to update systems that people now expect to be constantly available

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

One of Australia’s top intelligence agencies has warned that AI attacks could exploit the country’s old technology, as the government negotiates its guardrails on artificial intelligence’s rapid development.

The chief of Anthropic, developer of Claude, has warned AI bots could swarm the internet within a year and called to “slow the pace” of development with support from the head of OpenAI and Elon Musk.

Abigail Bradshaw, the director general of the Australian Signals Directorate, said her agency did not know how many AI agents were active on the internet.

“I think that prospect of getting some sort of definition or calculation of how these agents are out there is really remote,” Bradshaw said while speaking to the Sydney Dialogue summit in Canberra on Monday.

She said Australian governments and businesses would have to spend “enormous” amounts to update their vulnerable outdated technology, taking offline systems that Australians had come to expect would be available all the time.

Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, recently called for independent assessors to interrogate AI companies’ models and for US government permission for leading AI companies to coordinate without being punished for anti-competitive collusion. Bradshaw called for national security agencies to be involved in the independent interrogation.

The Greens demanded the government legislate mandatory safety testing and transparency obligations for the most developed AI systems on Monday but their motion for debate was rejected by Labor senators.

Labor’s Andrew Charlton, the assistant technology minister, told the Sydney Dialogue he took the companies’ warnings seriously but did not want them or the US to be responsible for setting the guardrails around AI.

“I don’t think we should care very much about what individual chief executives say or what individual executives claim they want to happen,” Charlton said.

Charlton said the Albanese government would set its forthcoming guidelines for AI companies to cover the range of “extremely dangerous” and more benign possibilities being forecast.

The laws are expected early next year. Anthropic’s chief lawyer, Jeff Bleich, told Monday’s summit the company had been “heartened” by the strong support for its calls and said Australia would need to play a role in setting the rules.

“I don’t think it makes any sense that something this important would be decided either by company executives or by leaders in only two countries,” Bleich said.

“It’s just important for the model developers not just for social licence, which is critical, but also some legal certainty.

“It won’t be easy to get these things done but it actually makes it better to come to Australia.”

But Bleich said Anthropic believed rules were needed within months as the technology developed at an exponential pace.

One of the factors affecting companies’ interest in Australia has been access to copyright-protected material produced by local creatives so it can train its models. The industry minister, Tim Ayres, told the summit the government wanted local training but remained unwilling to reduce copyright protections.

OpenAI’s vice-president for global policy, Ann O’Leary, said her company was in “regular” and “deep” conversation with the government about the copyright rules but was “very eager to have a bigger and broader relationship”.

“I don’t have to tell any of you how important Australia is from a geopolitical standpoint,” O’Leary told the summit. “We very much recognise that having a diversification of where we train is going to be important as you move forward.”

She said OpenAI wanted to ensure creators could keep creating.

Andrew Hastie, the Coalition’s industry spokesperson, warned the summit Australia would be vulnerable in future conflicts if it could not get advanced companies to locate themselves in Australia, calling for a formal deal with the US.

The government is already using Claude’s advanced Mythos model. Paul Robards, a data expert at Australia’s department of defence, downplayed the likelihood of Australia developing frontier technology.

“Without a sovereign AI frontier model here in Australia, we are going to be a supplicant state, not a sovereign state,” Hastie said.

“We need to work on a way to get a hyperscaler down under … I think working with the United States, through Aukus if we want to use that frame, is the pathway.”

title: Who has made Troy's Premier League team of the week?
description: After every round of Premier League matches this season, Troy Deeney gives us his team of the week. Do you agree with his choices?
fullText:
After every round of Premier League matches this season, BBC football pundit Troy Deeney will give you his team and manager of the week.

Here are this week's choices. Do you agree? Give us your thoughts using the comments form at the bottom of this page.

Gianluigi Donnarumma (Manchester City): Not only is he one of the best goalkeepers in the world, but he is a big-match player. We've seen it year on year and he's just won Manchester City two extra points against Manchester United. He'll get them 10 points over the course of the season, he's that good. After the Community Shield, people were saying he wasn't good enough and they should have kept James Trafford, but he proved again why he's such a big-time goalkeeper.

Daniel Munoz (Nottingham Forest): I thought he was a breath of fresh air in the win at Villa. No-one in that Forest team can do what he does. Pace, power, he can defend and offers you a lot going forward. I thought he was a steal. I can't believe Liverpool and Manchester United didn't go for him. Forest did unbelievable business getting him.

Ezri Konsa (Arsenal): Had a tough old battle against Brian Brobbey as they beat Sunderland. Last season, he ended up bullying Gabriel for the equaliser and he wanted no part of it. Konsa said 'no problem' and stepped up. That penalty was never a penalty.

Lewis Dunk (Brighton): Who knew the big 6ft 5in centre-half could put one in to the top bins, straight off the crossbar? Unbelievable. He goes in just for that strike against Coventry alone.

Tarik Muharemovic (Leeds United): What a beast he is. I don't know where Leeds found him but he heads it, kicks it, runs through people. Didn't get the clean sheet against Newcastle but deserved it.

Leif Davis (Ipswich Town): Very, very good. Very underrated. He delivered in a six-pointer because I think Palace are going to be down there, with a goal and an assist.

Enzo Fernandez (Manchester City): He had his best game in the last two years against Manchester United. He actually did everything the team needed - ran with the ball, looked after it, bought fouls, tried his best to get others sent off. I thought he was a catalyst for the team. His best performance for City so far.

Pascal Gross (Brighton): Goal and assists. The old head who they brought back steadies that ship - it's a really young team. He is even more important now with no Welbeck, no Milner. He is in and is a steady hand.

Kevin Schade (Brentford): Two goals again at Bournemouth. I feel like he's the next one they'll sell. Pace, power, scores goals and works hard for the team.

Mohamed Belloumi (Hull City): Was decent in the Championship but he's really taken to the Premier League. Looks like he's stepped up and thought he'll have a bit of this. Two goals away at Chelsea is huge. They probably felt like they should have won.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin (Leeds United): Steady away, isn't he? Goes about his business. Got one goal against Newcastle, should have had two. Excellent as a forward. Leeds have done something to keep him fit and he's changed the mentality for sticking in there. Maybe it's the Elland Road factor. They won't allow for anyone to not give 100%. He stays in the game all the time.

Enzo Maresca (Manchester City): An honourable mention for Mikel Arteta. Got the job done away again. We could have had Daniel Farke. We'll give it to Maresca. I'm not his biggest fan, but tactically he got it right at Old Trafford. He understood the moment and gave his team the best platform to do what they needed to win. Made a brave call in bringing Cherki off for Ndiaye.

title: 'Unplayable' & 'almost perfect' - Calvert-Lewin set for England recall?
description: Dominic Calvert-Lewin has now scored in Leeds' past five league matches. Is he ready for an England recall?
fullText:
Newcastle United must be sick of the sight of Dominic Calvert-Lewin.

The Leeds United striker has now scored eight times against the club he was previously linked with in years gone by.

So you suspect the beleaguered visitors will have been a little relieved to see him substituted late on after he had a hand in two of Leeds' goals in this impressive 4-1 win.

Elland Road was unsurprisingly on its feet to hand Calvert-Lewin a deserved standing ovation when he came off.

On a night Leeds fans repeatedly taunted Newcastle for spending "all that money" with little return on Monday night, at least, it was a free transfer who caused the visitors real problems with a goal and an assist.

So is the 29-year-old making a case for an England recall?

Leeds manager Daniel Farke certainly thinks so as he threw his weight behind Calvert-Lewin and a number of others in his side with "English passports".

"He's a handful and tough for each and every defender," he said.

"He's difficult to play against. He's at a top fitness level. You can see he plays with confidence and a good rhythm, but also benefits from a really strong team and players who work for him.

"Dominic is a crucial player and if he shows this type of form, he's definitely one of the best strikers in this league. It's the best league in the world and that more or less sums up what I think about him as a player."

Leeds move third as they hit four against Newcastle

Calvert-Lewin stars but Botman struggles - player ratings for Leeds v Newcastle

Calvert-Lewin has been in England head coach Thomas Tuchel's thoughts in recent months.

The striker was previously called up by his country back in March after catching the eye in his debut season at Leeds.

However, after featuring for England against Uruguay during that particular international window, the striker ultimately missed out on the World Cup in the summer.

Ivan Toney and Ollie Watkins instead travelled as captain Harry Kane's deputies.

At a time when the marginally older pair are both playing in Saudi Arabia, Calvert-Lewin is staking his claim with his performances closer to home in this country.

He has scored three goals in his past four games as the Premier League's leading English striker - just as Tuchel prepares to name his squad on Friday for the upcoming Nations League fixtures against Spain and the Czech Republic.

He is also just the second Leeds player to score in five consecutive Premier League appearances at Elland Road after Mark Viduka between March and August 2003.

Such was Calvert-Lewin's hunger, he looked dumbfounded after learning his header for Leeds' second against Newcastle had been awarded to team-mate Jayden Bogle after it took a final touch off his team-mate.

Former England defender Jamie Carragher was among those watching on impressed following his "almost perfect" display.

"Maybe sometimes composure has let him down in his career, but not here," he told Sky Sports about the former Everton striker. "He was unplayable.

"It was right for him and Everton to make a fresh start. As an Evertonian you are probably thinking why didn't we keep him.

"Sometimes a move rejuvenates a player. He is the type of player you think as an ex-centre-back, I am glad I am not playing now."

Who has made Troy's Premier League team of the week?

No side will relish coming up against Calvert-Lewin and this aggressive Leeds outfit at Elland Road this season.

In fact, only Arsenal (52), Manchester City (50), Manchester United (45) and Bournemouth (37) have won more Premier League points in 2026 than Leeds United (35), with the Whites suffering just a single defeat across their past 13 league matches.

Yet Newcastle's implosion was remarkable as a young team were bullied and outfought.

Newcastle had previously made a good start under head coach Matthias Jaissle, following so much change in the summer, and were unbeaten in their opening five games in all competitions before this reality check.

But they have faced more shots than any other side in the Premier League.

However clinical Newcastle were in the opening weeks of the campaign, they mustered just eight efforts on target against Liverpool, Tottenham Hotspur and Bournemouth before their trip to Elland Road.

That was a dangerous cocktail going into this game.

What was most galling, though, was the visitors' failure to match Leeds' bite at a raucous Elland Road.

Jaissle's side crumbled and conceded three goals in a chastening 14-minute period in the first half.

It was a night the German manager swore in his post-match news conference to illustrate how low he felt.

"I don't want to point fingers and point any players out tonight," he said. "We were not matching as a team the level of intensity, the level of duel behaviours, the level of physicality.

"This is something we need to bring on the pitch in every match. This is non-negotiable. It should be the basic fundamentals of football.

"These are young lads. The learning curve needs to be fast."

For Calvert-Lewin and Leeds, however, this was a night to remember.

title: Graham & Ure make Pocognoli's first Scotland squad
description: Stoke City centre-half Luke Graham and Sevilla striker Robbie Ure will receive their first full Scotland call-ups on Tuesday when Sebastien Pocognoli names his first squad as head coach.
fullText:
Stoke City centre-half Luke Graham and Sevilla striker Robbie Ure will receive their first full Scotland call-ups on Tuesday when Sebastien Pocognoli names his first squad as head coach.

Graham was part of Scotland's pre-World Cup training camp in May after a breakthrough campaign with Dundee, winning the Scottish Premiership club's players' player and young player of the year awards.

The 22-year-old was an unused substitute in the country's send-off friendly win against Curacao, which was also Steve Clarke's last game in the dugout at Hampden Park.

The defender, who has three caps at under-21 level, has started strongly for The Potters in the Championship, who are unbeaten in their last four games, with Graham an ever-present.

Former Rangers academy product Ure was in demand across Europe after a free-scoring spell - 20 goals and three assists in 20 matches - that took Sirius to the top of the table in Sweden and it resulted in a £5.5m summer transfer to La Liga with Sevilla.

Time for Pocognoli to pick - who could be named in new-look Scotland squad?

Stoke best place for me to take step up - Graham

Is Sevilla's 'all-round striker' Ure ready to lead Scotland's attack?

Ure, also 22, has yet to find the target in Spain, but given his eligibility for Ukraine, the new head coach appears tempted to tie him down as soon as possible as he is set to be named in the Belgian's squad when it will be announced at 11:00 (BST).

Since Poconogli was announced as Clarke's successor - after the former Kilmarnock manager resigned after the Scots failed to qualify for the knockout stages of a major tournament for the first time - the expectation has been that the Belgian will look to freshen up an ageing squad.

His countryman, Heart of Midlothian head coach Wouter Vrancken, is "confident" there will also be a few players from the Gorgie club included.

His front three of striker James Wilson and wingers Calvin Miller and Josh McPake have been receiving plaudits for their recent performances.

Former Scotland captain Scott Brown too has high hopes for the Hearts wingers who have heavily contributed to their side's strong start to the season.

Pocognoli will take charge of Scotland for the first time on Saturday, 26 September in the Scots' Nations League B opener against Slovenia and his debut in the Hampden dugout will be three days later against Switzerland.

fullText:
Republican Greg Abbott says datacenters must help ‘protect’ drought-prone state and disclose water use

Greg Abbott, the Texas governor, has directed state regulators to penalize datacenters that fail to comply with state laws requiring them to disclose their water use.

“Data centers must share the duty to protect Texas water,” the Republican governor said on Monday. “The Texas Water Code requires a complete and accurate water use survey. I direct the Texas Water Development Board to use its enforcement authority to penalize past failures and to impose legal consequences for any future failure to comply,” he added.

In a letter to the water board, Abbott, who is seeking a fourth term, said: “Major water users, including data centers, appear to have committed civil and criminal violations by failing to provide the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) with information about water usage as required by the Texas Water Code.”

It follows a directive Abbott issued last month ordering the Public Utility Commission of Texas and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (Ercot) to conduct a comprehensive audit of datacenters advancing through the Ercot interconnection process.

Drought-prone Texas has fast become the heart of the US’s datacenter boom.

Texas has the second-most datacenters of any state in the country, according to a tally by the Pew Research Center. But with 335 datacenters, and at least 248 

But, amid growing public concern over datacenter construction, Texas has been working to tighten oversight of the industry as demand grows for the state’s power and water supplies.

In 2025, Texas datacenters consumed an estimated 25bn gallons of water, according to the Houston Advanced Research Center. Water use by datacenters in the state could rise to 161bn gallons a year by 2030 – about 2.7% of all water used in Texas, or roughly the amount consumed by 1.3m households across the country.

The audit requires datacenters to provide information about their water consumption, water sources and efforts to use water-efficient technologies. Abbott said projects that fail to complete the audit will be denied permission to connect to the state’s power grid.

“TWDB’s water use surveys serve a similarly important purpose as this data center audit. TWDB must coordinate with PUC and ERCOT to ensure that covered entities provide critical water use information in response,” Abbott said in his Monday letter. “Any failure to respond to the audit’s request for water use information would trigger TWDB’s independent enforcement authority.”
